knowledge:
- key_parameters: pValues=A numerical vector of p-values to be analyzed ;; X=A design matrix, data frame, or vector containing numeric covariates (no factors or categorical variables allowed directly) ;; truncated=A vector of 0s and 1s indicating if a p-value is truncated (e.g., p < 0.01) ;; rounded=A vector of 0s and 1s indicating if a p-value is rounded ;; type=The regression model type, either "logistic" (default and recommended) or "linear" ;; smoothing=The spline-fitting algorithm, either "unit.spline" (default, fast) or "smooth.spline" (exact parity with the qvalue package but slower) ;; smooth.df=Degrees of freedom for spline smoothing (default is 3, must be >= 3) ;; threshold=If TRUE (default), forces pi0 predictions to lie within the [0, 1] range
- alternatives: qvalue=The classic qvalue package (via the qvalue function) is preferred when all statistical tests are a-priori similar and no covariate metadata is available ;; Bonferroni correction=A conservative alternative that controls family-wise error rate but leads to a high rate of false negatives compared to FDR-based methods
- when_to_use: Use covariate-conditioned workflows when performing large-scale multiple testing (e.g., GWAS or differential expression) where metadata (like sample size or allele frequency) can inform the prior probability of a null hypothesis being true. Use the swfdr workflow when estimating the false positive rate of published scientific literature using web-scraped or reported p-values.
- pitfalls: Covariate matrix X must contain only numeric data; factors and categorical variables must be pre-processed into dummy variables (e.g., using model.matrix) ;; Covariate matrix X cannot contain missing (NA) or non-finite (NULL, Inf, NaN) values ;; For small datasets (e.g., under 100 tests), the default lambda vector may be too long and should be manually shortened to avoid spline fitting issues ;; Using smoothing="smooth.spline" on large datasets significantly increases computation time compared to the default "unit.spline"

workflows.name: covariate_conditioned_fdr
workflows.intent: Estimate the proportion of true null hypotheses and compute adjusted q-values while conditioning on one or more numeric covariates.
input: BMI_GIANT_GWAS_sample (a data frame containing a column of p-values and columns of metadata covariates like sample size N and allele frequency Freq_MAF_Int_Hapmap)
workflows.stages: 1. Construct a numeric design matrix from covariates using model.matrix ;; 2. Estimate the conditional proportion of nulls (pi0) using lm_pi0 ;; 3. Compute conditional q-values using lm_qvalue
workflows.code:
X <- model.matrix(~ splines::ns(N,5) + Freq_MAF_Int_Hapmap, data = BMI_GIANT_GWAS_sample)[,-1]
pi0x <- lm_pi0(BMI_GIANT_GWAS_sample$p, X=X)
GWAS_lm_qvalue <- lm_qvalue(GWAS$p, X=GWAS[, c("N", "Freq_MAF_Hapmap")])

workflows.name: science_wise_fdr_estimation
workflows.intent: Estimate the science-wise false discovery rate from published literature p-values, accounting for rounding and truncation.
input: journals_pVals (a data frame containing published p-values and truncation status metadata)
workflows.stages: 1. Filter the dataset to keep only p-values below 0.05 ;; 2. Define vectors indicating truncation and rounding status ;; 3. Run the EM algorithm using calculateSwfdr to estimate the overall false discovery rate (pi0)
workflows.code:
journals_pVals1 <- dplyr::filter(journals_pVals,
                                 year == 2005,
                                 journal == "American Journal of Epidemiology",
                                 pvalue < 0.05)
tt <- data.frame(journals_pVals1)[,2]
rr <- rep(0,length(tt))
rr[tt == 0] <- (data.frame(journals_pVals1)[tt==0,1] == 
                  round(data.frame(journals_pVals1)[tt==0,1],2))
pVals <- data.frame(journals_pVals1)[,1]
resSwfdr <- calculateSwfdr(pValues = pVals, 
                           truncated = tt, 
                           rounded = rr, numEmIterations=100)
